title: Number Sense and Place Value: Millions to Thousandths

pedagogy.rationale: Learners meet place value through a chart and counters (concrete/pictorial) before reading, writing and comparing numbers symbolically. Grade 7 extends the whole-number chart learners know to the thousandths, which the MOE Grade 7 decimals, percents and fractions period depends on.

prerequisiteAssumptions: Can read and write whole numbers to at least 100,000 (MOE Grade 4 numeration).
Knows that 0.5 means five tenths and can read simple decimals aloud.
Can multiply a single digit by 10, 100 and 1,000.

misconceptions.description: Gives the digit itself (3) instead of its value in the number (300,000).
misconceptions.response: Ask two questions every time: which place is the digit in, and what is one of that place worth? Then multiply.

misconceptions.description: Leaves out zeros that hold empty places, writing three million, sixty thousand, five hundred as 3,600,500.
misconceptions.response: Write the number in a place-value chart first; every column must hold a digit, even if it is 0.

misconceptions.description: Writes 'four and six hundredths' as 4.6, ignoring the place the fraction name gives.
misconceptions.response: The fraction name tells you the last place: hundredths ends two places after the point, so 4.06.

misconceptions.description: Thinks a decimal with more digits is greater (0.45 > 0.5 because 45 > 5).
misconceptions.response: Line up the decimal points, fill empty places with zeros (0.50 and 0.45) and compare from the left.

scenes.title: Big and small numbers in everyday Liberia
scenes.learnerAction: Read the two numbers and think about which digit is worth the most in each.

content.body:
Musu's school raised **L$2,350,480** for a new library. At the market, a trader weighs **2.375 kg** of rice for a customer. One number is in the millions. The other has parts smaller than one.

Both numbers follow the same rule: **where a digit sits decides what it is worth**. In this lesson you will use that rule to read, write and compare numbers from the millions down to the thousandths.

scenes.title: Warm-up: what do you remember?
scenes.learnerAction: Answer two quick questions from earlier grades and read the feedback.

content.body: Before we start, check what you already know from earlier grades. These answers are not marked. They show you where to focus today.

options.feedback: That is the digit itself. Its place makes it worth more: the 3 is in the hundreds place, so it is worth 300.
Yes. The 3 is in the hundreds place, so it is worth 3 × 100 = 300.
30 would need the 3 in the tens place. Count from the right: ones (4), tens (8), hundreds (3).
Yes. The first place after the decimal point is the tenths place, so 0.5 is 5 tenths.
5 hundredths is written 0.05. In 0.5 the 5 is in the first place after the point: tenths.
5 ones is just 5. The decimal point shows that this 5 is smaller than one.

hints: Name each place, starting from the ones place.

scenes.title: The place-value chart: millions to thousandths
scenes.learnerAction: Study the chart and read the number 4,205,316.27 aloud.

content.body:
Every digit has a **place** (its position) and a **value** (what it is worth in that place).

Left of the decimal point, digits are grouped in threes called **periods**: ones, thousands and millions. Commas separate the periods. Right of the decimal point are the **tenths**, **hundredths** and **thousandths**.

In **4,205,316.27** the 4 is in the millions place, so it is worth 4,000,000. The 0 holds the ten-thousands place: there are no ten thousands. The 2 after the point is in the tenths place, so it is worth 0.2.
keyPoints: Read one period at a time, then say its name: four million, two hundred five thousand, three hundred sixteen.
Read the decimal part by its last place: and twenty-seven hundredths. In class you may also hear four million ... sixteen point two seven.
A zero holds an empty place so every other digit stays where it belongs.

scenes.title: Each place is worth ten times the next
scenes.learnerAction: Open each step in order to follow the × 10 and ÷ 10 pattern.

content.body: Places are not random. Open each step to see how every place is connected to its neighbours.

steps.label: Start at the ones
steps.description: One one is worth 1. This is the place everything else is measured from.

steps.label: Move left: multiply by 10
steps.description: 1 ten = 10 ones = 10. 1 hundred = 10 tens = 100. Each step to the left makes a place worth 10 times more.

steps.label: Keep going to the millions
steps.description: 1 thousand = 1,000. 1 ten thousand = 10,000. 1 hundred thousand = 100,000. 1 million = 1,000,000: six steps of × 10 from the ones.

steps.label: Move right: divide by 10
steps.description: 1 tenth = 1 ÷ 10 = 0.1. A tenth is ten times smaller than one.

steps.label: Hundredths and thousandths
steps.description: 1 hundredth = 0.01 and 1 thousandth = 0.001. Each step to the right divides by 10 again.

steps.label: Same digit, different values
steps.description: In 5,555.555 every digit is a 5, but the values are 5,000, 500, 50, 5, 0.5, 0.05 and 0.005.

media.description: A ladder of places from millions down to thousandths with × 10 arrows going up and ÷ 10 arrows going down.
media.altText: Ladder of place values: 1,000,000; 100,000; 10,000; 1,000; 100; 10; 1; 0.1; 0.01; 0.001. Each rung is 10 times the rung below it.

hints: Moving left multiplies by 10; moving right divides by 10.

accessibility.textAlternative: Six steps, each a button that opens text: values grow by × 10 to the left (up to 1,000,000) and shrink by ÷ 10 to the right (down to 0.001).

scenes.title: Worked example: Musu's library fund
scenes.learnerAction: Open each step of the worked example and check it against the chart.

content.body: Musu's school collected **L$2,350,480**. Musu's teacher asks three questions about the number. Open each step to see how to answer them.

steps.label: What is the 3 worth?
steps.description: Name the places from the left: millions (2), hundred thousands (3). The 3 is worth 3 × 100,000 = 300,000.

steps.label: Write it in expanded form
steps.description: 2,000,000 + 300,000 + 50,000 + 400 + 80. The zeros in the thousands and ones places are not written as parts.

steps.label: Write it in words
steps.description: Two million, three hundred fifty thousand, four hundred eighty Liberian dollars.

steps.label: Check by adding the parts
steps.description: 2,000,000 + 300,000 + 50,000 + 400 + 80 = 2,350,480. The parts add back to the number, so the expanded form is right.

hints: Name the place before you say the value.

scenes.title: Build a number
scenes.learnerAction: Place each digit in a place-value chart, then write the number you built.

content.body: Numbers are built from digits in places. Draw a place-value chart from the millions to the thousandths and build this number. Remember: a place with nothing in it still needs a **zero**.
keyPoints: 3 millions, 4 hundred thousands, 0 ten thousands, 6 thousands

interaction.prompt: Build the number from its places, then enter it in standard form.

fallback.content: Write the number you built in standard form, with commas between the periods and a decimal point. You can use stones or bottle caps as counters on your paper chart.

scenes.title: Guided practice: digits after the point
scenes.learnerAction: Answer two questions about decimal places and read the feedback after each one.

content.body: Use the chart. Name the place first, then give the value. Read the feedback after each answer before you move on.

options.feedback: 7 would be in the ones place. The 7 is two places after the decimal point.
0.7 is 7 tenths. Count the places after the point: tenths (2), hundredths (7).
Yes. The 7 is in the hundredths place, so it is worth 7 hundredths, which is 0.07.
70 would need the 7 in the tens place, left of the point.
Check the 8: it is the third digit after the point, the thousandths place, so it is 0.008.
Yes. 6 ones, 4 tenths, 0 hundredths and 8 thousandths. The zero is not written as a part.
Each digit after the point is worth less than one. The 4 is 4 tenths, not 4.

hints: After the point the places are tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

scenes.title: How to compare and order numbers
scenes.learnerAction: Open each step to follow the compare-from-the-left method.

content.body: To compare numbers, compare their places, not how many digits they have. Open each step to order **0.5**, **0.45** and **0.405**.

steps.label: Line up the places
steps.description: Write the numbers one under the other with the decimal points in a column. Fill empty places with zeros: 0.500, 0.450, 0.405.

steps.label: Compare from the left
steps.description: Start at the greatest place. The ones are all 0, so look at the tenths: 5, 4 and 4.

steps.label: The first different digit decides
steps.description: 5 tenths is the most, so 0.5 is the greatest. 0.450 and 0.405 tie in the tenths. In the hundredths 5 is more than 0, so 0.45 is greater than 0.405.

steps.label: Whole numbers work the same way
steps.description: 4,099,999 and 4,100,000 both have 4 millions. In the hundred thousands 0 is less than 1, so 4,099,999 is less than 4,100,000, even with all its nines.

media.description: 0.500, 0.450 and 0.405 lined up in a tenths-hundredths-thousandths chart, with the first different digit outlined, beside two hundredths grids shading 50 and 45 squares.
media.altText: 0.500, 0.450 and 0.405 lined up by place. Tenths: 5, 4, 4. Hundredths: 0, 5, 0. A hundredths grid shows 50 squares shaded for 0.5 and 45 squares for 0.45, so 0.5 is greater.

hints: Fill empty places with zeros so every number has the same number of decimal places.

scenes.title: Watch out: three common mistakes
scenes.learnerAction: Decide whether each claim is right, then read why.

content.body: Many learners make these three mistakes. Choose an answer for each one, then read the explanation.

items.prompt: Kollie says 0.45 is greater than 0.5 because 45 is greater than 5. Is he right?

options.feedback: Compare place by place instead. In the tenths place 0.5 has 5 tenths and 0.45 has only 4 tenths, so 0.5 is greater.
Right. Write 0.5 as 0.50: 50 hundredths is more than 45 hundredths. More digits does not mean a bigger number.

items.prompt: Which number is two million, forty thousand, seven hundred?

options.feedback: 2,400,700 has 4 hundred thousands. Forty thousand is 4 ten thousands, so the hundred-thousands place holds a zero.
Yes. The zero holds the hundred-thousands place so the 4 stays in the ten-thousands place.
240,700 has no millions. Two million needs a 2 in the millions place: 2,040,700.

items.prompt: How do you write four and six hundredths?

options.feedback: 4.6 is four and six tenths. Hundredths end two places after the point: 4.06.
Yes. The 6 is in the hundredths place, so the tenths place holds a zero.
4.600 is the same as 4.6, which is six tenths, not six hundredths.

hints: Use the chart: put each digit in its column before deciding.

feedback.onStruggle: Go back to the chart scene and place each number in the columns.

accessibility.textAlternative: Three misconception checks: whether 0.45 is greater than 0.5, writing two million forty thousand seven hundred, and writing four and six hundredths.

scenes.title: Your turn: independent practice
scenes.learnerAction: Answer five questions on your own, then read the feedback.

content.body: Work on your own. Each answer shows why it is right or what to check again. Use the place-value chart in your exercise book if it helps.

items.prompt: What is the value of the 7 in 1,742,009?

options.feedback: 7,000 would need the 7 in the thousands place. Count from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, hundred thousands.
Yes. The 7 is in the hundred-thousands place, so it is worth 7 × 100,000 = 700,000.
70,000 is one place too far right. The 7 sits next to the millions digit.
Yes. 3 millions, 6 ten thousands and 5 hundreds. Zeros hold the empty places and are not written as parts.
Check where the 6 is: it is in the ten-thousands place, not the hundred-thousands place.
The first digit is in the millions place, so it is worth 3,000,000.

items.prompt: Which number is five million, forty thousand, nine?

options.feedback: Each period name (million, thousand) needs its own group of three digits.
Forty thousand is 40,000, not 400,000.
Yes. Five million is 5,000,000, forty thousand is 40,000 and nine is 9. Together: 5,040,009.

items.prompt: A farmers' cooperative sold 2.75 tonnes of cocoa in June and 2.705 tonnes in July. In which month did it sell more?

options.feedback: Yes. Both have 2 ones and 7 tenths. In the hundredths 5 is more than 0, so 2.75 is greater than 2.705.
More digits does not mean more. Compare place by place: the hundredths are 5 and 0, so June is greater.
They share 2 ones and 7 tenths, but the hundredths are different: 5 and 0.
4 would be in the ones place. The 4 is the third digit after the point.
0.04 is 4 hundredths. The 4 is one place further right.
Yes. The 4 is in the thousandths place, so it is worth 4 thousandths, which is 0.004.
0.4 is 4 tenths, the first place after the point. Here the 3 is in the tenths place.

hints: Name the place, then the value.
To compare, line up the places and look from the left.

feedback.onStruggle: Review the chart and the compare steps, then try the questions again.

scenes.title: Key ideas to remember
scenes.learnerAction: Read the four key ideas before the exit ticket.

content.body: Before the exit ticket, review the big ideas of this lesson.
keyPoints: The value of a digit depends on its place: in 2,350,480 the 3 is worth 300,000.
Each place is worth 10 times the place to its right, from the thousandths up to the millions.
Zeros hold empty places: three million, sixty thousand, five hundred is 3,060,500.
To compare, line up the places and look from the left. The first different digit decides: 0.5 is greater than 0.45.
